newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S. UNBENDING ON NATO DISPUTE WITH FRANCE.
newsitem.headline: U.S. UNBENDING ON NATO DISPUTE WITH FRANCE.

text.p: State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Tuesday the United States had not changed its stance over who should head NATO's southern commmand, insisting the Naples-based post should remain in American hands.

"The American position has not changed. The commander of AFSOUTH, the NATO command, must be an American," Burns told reporters on the sidelines of a Paris summit marking the signing of a NATO-Russia pact.

France, which left the North Atlanttic Treaty Organisation's integrated military command in 1966, has been pressing for the Naples position, traditionally held by an American admiral, to be handed over to a European officer.

Paris says the change, or at least an equal sharing of responsibility, is essential to create a European defence identity and its own move to return fully to NATO's military command will be frozen unless a satisfactory accord is reached.
"The Americans want to see France return wholly to the alliance in every way, including in all military respects. We have this issue under continual review," Burns said.

"But the issue has still not been resolved. It is an important issue that we do want to see resolved and we have discussed a variety of possible solutions with the French but did not agree on any of them," he said.

"Our position is that in a military structure it is very difficult to share a command. NATO has a hierarchy, has commanders and we believe the United States should retain that command because our fleet, the Sixth Fleet, is the major military asset of that command," Burns said.
"How could a major American fleet be commanded by a foreigner? It would be quite unusual," he said.
French officials have stressed they are not seeking European control over the nuclear-armed Sixth Fleet, which they say could be put directly under NATO's American Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.

Burns said Washington wanted a greater European role in NATO commands but declined to go into details, except to say that the United States did not agree that the Sixth Fleet should be separated from the Naples command.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright discussed the issue on Monday with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.

French officials have indicated in recent weeks that the issue did not demand an immediate solution, a way to avoid a possible conflict at a NATO summit in Madrid in July, which is due to invite the first former communist east European countries to join the alliance.
Uncertainty about the outcome of France's parliamentary election, which goes into a decisive second round next Sunday, may also affect the issue.

If the left-wing opposition wins and shares power with conservative Gaullist President Jacques Chirac, the prime mover behind France's rapprochement with NATO, that process is likely to be frozen or even halted entirely.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin is wary of a full return to the NATO fold and has accused Chirac of giving in to the United States without getting anything in return. The Socialists' Communist partners are militantly opposed to rejoining NATO's military command.
